text: The Digital Ceasefire & Deescalation Handbook provides a framework and language that Parties can use to negotiate and mediate the Digital components of Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances. It was drafted to reflect the increasing digitalization of contemporary conflict, ensuring that any agreement binding Parties to cease prohibited acts includes appropriate language that addresses this reality.

The Handbook uses the term Prohibited Digital Operations, defined as Digital acts the Parties agree to cease which can be carried out in the context of an Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance.

Even though an agreement between Parties to cease Prohibited Digital Operations might take different forms, the structure of this Handbook is modeled after and adapted from traditional ceasefire agreements, including provisions such as preamble; entry into force; prohibited acts; third parties; permissible acts; monitoring body; definitions; and signatories. All words that are capitalized in this Note to Users and in the Handbook are defined at the end of the Handbook.

In the context of an Armed Conflict, this Handbook contains model language addressing Prohibited Digital Operations that may be incorporated into a traditional ceasefire agreement, appended as an annex to a ceasefire agreement, or used to negotiate a standalone Digital ceasefire agreement.

In situations of Grey Zone Activities or Internal Disturbances, where there is no Armed Conflict present, Parties may similarly wish to deescalate Digital conflict by including Handbook provisions in another form of agreement, such as a political agreement or code of conduct, or as Confidence Building Measures in an existing agreement.
This Handbook divides Prohibited Digital Operations into three categories:

1. Internet Interference, which may include Internet Shutdowns, Internet Infrastructure Attacks, and Electronic Jamming; 2. Information Threats, which may include Misinformation, Disinformation, Manipulated Media, Hate Speech, Online Incitement to Violence, Deepfakes, Doxxing, Online Advertisements, and Online Recruitment; and 3. Cyber Attacks, which may include Denial of Service Attacks, Hacking, and the use of Malware, Phishing, Spyware, and Surveillance technologies.

Certain provisions in this Handbook may be difficult – and some may believe, impossible – for Parties to agree to and/or implement. For instance, Parties may be reluctant to be monitored for breaches to an agreement. If Parties do agree to a monitoring body, Cyber Attacks and Information Threats often cannot be attributed with 100% certainty, particularly when acts are committed by Proxy Actors.

Because Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Companies’ products and services contribute to Cyber Attacks, Internet Interference, and Information Threats, they may be considered actors in the conflict even if they are not Parties to the agreement, but binding them to terms will be difficult and collaboration with them may not be easy.

Additionally, there may be differing views on whether an agreement should be reached on certain provisions in this Handbook. For instance, Cyber Attacks against Digital Infrastructure may be used by some Parties instead of kinetic attacks on physical infrastructure, and there may be concern that banning Cyber Attacks under an agreement may then escalate a situation.

Despite these challenges, States, non-State actors, mediators, negotiators, and civilians affected by Digital unrest have expressed the real need for guidance about how to address the use of new technologies in different conflict scenarios.

This is a forward-looking Handbook that is designed to provide Parties with a menu of options they can pick and choose from to fit their particular context, whether it is an international or non-international Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, or an Internal Disturbance.

The text of this Handbook is based on a combination of academic research, primary source interviews, international organization and nonprofit analysis, and a review of historical and existing ceasefire and peace agreements. Consultations with experts, diplomats, advisors, people on the ground in conflicts, and Parties currently or previously engaged in negotiation processes is ongoing to ensure that the provisions proposed directly meet the needs of current conflicts and domestic unrest.

The Agreement is informed by the excellent work of multiple actors who are cited throughout including [Access Now](http://Accessnow.org), [Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue (HD)](https://hdcentre.org/), [PA-X Peace Agreements Database](https://www.peaceagreements.org/), [Build Up](https://howtobuildup.org/), [Public International Law and Policy Group (PILPG)](https://www.publicinternationallawandpolicygroup.org/), [International Committee of the Red Cross](https://www.icrc.org/en), and the [UN Mediation Support Unit (MSU)](https://peacemaker.un.org/en/mediation-support-unit/mediation-support-unit). The document was developed with reference to PILPG’s Ceasefire Drafter’s Handbook.

The authors recommend that Parties using this Handbook engage with technical experts who understand the Digital elements of the conflict, the technologies being used, and how such uses might be monitored and verified. The authors also recommend scoping the full range of hostilities, both Digital and non-Digital, so Parties can address both or complement existing negotiations.

For further information, guidance, or training the drafters of this Agreement are available and can be contacted: Brett Solomon ([contact@brettsolomon.info](mailto:contact@brettsolomon.info)) and Betsy Popken ([bpopken@berkeley.edu](mailto:bpopken@berkeley.edu)) of the [Digital Ceasefire Initiative](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/projects/digital-ceasefire-initiative/) at the [Human Rights Center, UC Berkeley](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/).
WE, the Parties to this Agreement, [Party A, Party B, ... ]:
RECOGNIZING that the {{o-context}} includes both traditional and Digital dimensions;
COMMITTED to understanding the nature, scope, harm, and cause of Prohibited Digital Operations in the drafting and successful implementation of this Agreement;
RECOGNIZING that Prohibited Digital Operations can be carried out in the context of an Armed Conflict, in the Grey Zone, and in Internal Disturbances;
DETERMINED to address Prohibited Digital Operations that most affect civilians;

MINDFUL of the importance of reducing traditional barriers to participation, such as geography, gender, language, and literacy by including all relevant sectors in the drafting and implementation of this Agreement;

RECOGNIZING the role that Third Party cyber groups, political forces, private Information and Communication Technology Companies, and civil society organizations can play in contributing to the success of this Agreement or undermining it;
RECOGNIZING that there may be participants in the conflict that are not Parties to this Agreement, yet critical to its success;
COMMITTED to the full, complete, and permanent end to the {{o-context}};
COMMITTED to upholding International Law and to promoting full respect for International Humanitarian Law, International Criminal Law, and International Human Rights Law;
COMMITTED to protecting civilians, including respect for the rights of women, children, and other vulnerable groups, and to protect civilian infrastructure and private and public property;

RECOGNIZING that access to the internet and other Digital means of information sharing and communication is essential to protecting rights and that people’s lives, security, and wellbeing rely upon that access, particularly during times of {{o-context}};
RECOGNIZING that the same rights that people have offline must also be protected online;

APPRECIATING that the use of technologies and the technologies used in {{o-context}} are evolving quickly and that those not explicitly named in this Agreement may be subject to its provisions or the Parties may subsequently amend this Agreement to include them;
OBSERVING that while not all Prohibited Digital Operations have an immediate or direct impact on civilians, there are often secondary effects that cause harm, physical damage, or death;

RECOGNIZING the role women play in the Digital sphere as advocates of peace on and offline, as well as the heightened danger and insecurity that women often face online due to threats from Deepfakes and as the subject of Misinformation and Disinformation;

RECOGNIZING that Digital harms impact intersectional identities differently – including but not limited to gender, class, religion, ability, ethnicity, sexual orientation, age, and migration status – and therefore an inclusive, context-specific approach is needed to address these harms;

ACKNOWLEDGING that where this Agreement is incorporated into or annexed to an agreement governing non-Digital aspects of {{o-context}}, its breach constitutes a breach of that agreement. Where there is a separate non-Digital agreement, it remains binding and operates in parallel to this Agreement, and unless expressly provided, a breach of one does not constitute a breach of the other;
COMMITTED to all current and previous valid agreements between the Parties;
Hereby agree to be bound by the provisions.
The Parties agree to abide by the terms of this Agreement {{o-upon-signature-of-the}}.
The Agreement will remain in effect {{o-indefinitely}}.
The Parties agree to suspend all Prohibited Digital Operations for the duration of this ceasefire, as further specified below:

Prohibited Digital Operations include attacks against civilians and Civilian Objects, both of which remain protected under International Humanitarian Law irrespective of this Agreement. This includes any operation intended to, or reasonably expected to, disable, disrupt, degrade, manipulate, or destroy civilian infrastructure or services.

Prohibited Digital Operations also include attacks against Military Objectives. This prohibition applies irrespective of whether such operations would otherwise be lawful under International Humanitarian Law.

Parties shall not conduct Prohibited Digital Operations against Dual-Use objects that serve both civilian and military purposes where such operations would be expected to cause harm to civilians, Civilian Objects, or civilian infrastructure. In cases of uncertainty, objects shall be presumed to be civilian.
No Party to this Agreement shall use, conduct, engage in, or initiate the following acts of Internet Interference:
The Parties shall not intentionally disrupt or shut down access to the internet, in whole or in part, including efforts to disconnect the other Party from the global internet.

Parties shall refrain from taking any measures that result in Internet Shutdowns or disruption of internet services – including Throttling or blocking of key websites, applications, or platforms – within the territories under their control, including occupied territories or in sovereign jurisdictions where such shutdowns or disruptions can be executed. This includes any acts that would hinder access to online communications, humanitarian services, information sharing, public discourse, personal financial resources, or other essential services that rely on the internet.
The Parties agree that no Party to this Agreement shall damage or disrupt the Public Core or availability of the internet.

The Parties shall refrain from conducting Cyber Operations or physical attacks causing destruction, damage, or seizure of communications infrastructure, including but not limited to internet exchange points, data centers, undersea cables, satellite and space-based internet services, broadcast facilities, and telecommunications towers, which impacts peoples’ ability to access the internet. The Parties shall cease the manipulation of internet routing, domain name systems, and traffic exchange mechanisms.

The Parties shall refrain from Electronic Jamming, signal interference, or other electromagnetic actions intended to disrupt, degrade, or deny access to communications networks or services, including radio, satellite, mobile, and internet connectivity.

The Parties shall not direct, support, or knowingly permit interference with internet availability by Third Parties, and shall take reasonable measures to prevent such interference from their territory or through infrastructure under their control.

The Parties shall not interfere with the continued availability of internet and communications services necessary for humanitarian operations, medical services, emergency response, civilian warning systems, and access to essential public information.
No Party to this Agreement shall use, conduct, engage in, or initiate the following acts of Information Threats:
All Parties agree not to knowingly disseminate or amplify Misinformation or create, disseminate, or amplify Disinformation which may escalate hostilities, incite violence, or undermine peace efforts.

Parties agree that content prohibited under this Agreement includes the fabrication or distortion of significant facts – such as an announcement of a false humanitarian corridor, the incorrect location of conflict zones, impersonation of political officials or organizations, encouraging civilians to stand against peace, smear campaigns against protestors and peace negotiators, and the hostile manipulation of public perception.
Parties agree that spreading distrust in the Parties to the Agreement, the process that developed the Agreement, and the Digital Monitoring Commission is prohibited under this Agreement.

This shall not be interpreted to restrict lawful expression, including political speech, satire, journalism, or criticism. It applies to deliberate Misinformation and Disinformation intended to incite violence, undermine peace efforts, or escalate the conflict, and must be applied consistently with International Human Rights Law, including Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

Parties agree not to create, distribute, or endorse manipulated or synthetic media, such as deep fake photographs or images and manipulated videos, where there is an imminent risk of it leading to or inciting violence. This provision expressly prohibits content that leads to or incites sexual and gender-based violence.

Parties shall refrain from manipulating platform algorithms, recommendation systems, engagement metrics, or other Digital systems in a manner intended to artificially amplify deceptive, divisive, or violent content, or to distort the visibility, reach, or credibility of information online.

Parties shall not create, deploy, coordinate, or support fake accounts, automated bot networks, troll farms, synthetic identities, impersonation campaigns, or other forms of coordinated inauthentic behaviour intended to manipulate public discourse, deceive populations, impersonate persons or organisations, suppress participation, or undermine the peace process.
This shall not be interpreted to restrict lawful expression, including satire, parody, political commentary, or artistic expression, protected under International Law.
Parties agree to refrain from engaging in, facilitating, or enabling Doxxing of individuals or groups in a manner that endangers their safety, privacy, or well-being.

Parties agree to refrain from exposing any personally identifying details of civilians, journalists, humanitarian workers, peace negotiators, Parties, or other agreed persons in ways that could lead to harassment, intimidation, persecution, or physical harm.

All Parties shall refrain from engaging in or facilitating Online Incitement to Violence, including any form of online harassment, intimidation, provocation, or hatred toward any person or group of persons or their beliefs that may lead to violence. This prohibition includes accusations of apostasy, treason, terrorism, or any other similar charges.

Parties agree that content that fuels regionalist, racial, ethnic, sectarian, or tribal divisions that could threaten the peace are prohibited under this Agreement, as is content that targets specific individuals, including peacebuilders.

Parties agree to work independently and collaboratively, where appropriate, to ensure that social media and communications platforms are not used as tools for violence, radicalization, or societal unrest.
Parties agree to work, if possible, with social media and communications platforms to detect and remove content that may be in breach of this Agreement.
This shall not be interpreted to suppress legitimate criticism, debate, or dissent.

All Parties shall refrain from drafting, disseminating, promoting, or endorsing Hate Speech that incites, or has a reasonable probability to incite, discrimination, hostility, and violence. This prohibition extends to public statements, media, broadcast, and social media and communications platforms, as well as Hate Speech in the form of symbols, slogans, or imagery.
No Party shall accuse another Party of Hate Speech as a means to suppress dissent.
This shall not be interpreted to restrict legitimate expressions of opinion, criticism, or debate.
Parties agree not to engage in Online Recruitment of Cyber Mercenaries, hacktivist groups, terrorist organizations, child soldiers, criminal organizations, or private military contractors.
Parties agree not to pay for Online Advertisements that spread Misinformation, Disinformation, or otherwise undermine trust between the Parties and the likelihood of achieving peace.

The Parties shall not interfere with, manipulate, or falsify information or Data relating to humanitarian operations, including information or Data concerning civilians, aid delivery, or protected persons.
The Parties shall not target journalists, media organisations, or news platforms through information operations, including harassment, intimidation, or Disinformation campaigns.
The Parties agree that an agreement to cease Cyber Attacks against another Party does not enable a Party or Proxy Actor to use, conduct, engage in, or initiate any other form of kinetic attack.
No Party to this Agreement shall use, conduct, engage in, or initiate Cyber Attacks on the following persons or objects, or using the following means or methods:

The Parties shall refrain from conducting or facilitating unlawful or arbitrary Digital Surveillance activities, including the use or deployment of Spyware or other intrusive technologies that enable covert access to the devices, networks, communications, or Data of civilians, humanitarian actors, journalists, activists, or other protected persons.

The Parties shall not conduct Digital Surveillance, including the use of Spyware, against civilians, including their own populations, except pursuant to lawful authority, subject to judicial authorization, and in accordance with the principles of legality, necessity, proportionality, and effective oversight under applicable law and human rights norms.
The Parties reaffirm their obligation to respect the right to privacy of all individuals within and beyond their territory.

Parties agree to refrain from conducting or facilitating cyber intrusions, Hacking, or other forms of unauthorized access against official or personal devices of political actors, civil society, women’s groups, peace negotiators, others targeted for their identity, or the general public.

Parties shall refrain from manipulating, corrupting, poisoning, falsifying, deleting, or otherwise compromising the integrity or reliability of Data belonging to civilians, humanitarian actors, public institutions, or other protected persons or entities.

The Parties shall refrain from conducting or facilitating Cyber Operations against the military systems, networks, communications, or devices of other Parties that are intended to, or reasonably could be expected to, disrupt, degrade, manipulate, or impair the functioning, reliability, or control of such systems.

Parties agree to refrain from testing, deploying, distributing, transferring, or utilizing Malware, or any related tools, including ransomware and other extortion-based Cyber Operations, to compromise or disrupt the integrity, security, or functionality of any computer or Digital systems, networks, or Data belonging to other Parties to the Agreement.

This prohibition extends to civilians, the general public, journalists, media organizations, civil society actors, humanitarian personnel, political actors, peace negotiators, or individuals targeted on the basis of their identity.

All Parties agree not to conduct, support, or facilitate any Distributed Denial of Service Attacks against the computer systems, networks, or critical infrastructure of another Party. This prohibition includes any actions intended to disrupt, degrade, or render unavailable essential services and communications, Digital Infrastructure, and social media and communications platforms used by the public and Parties to the Agreement.
Parties agree that Phishing to obtain sensitive information about another Party, including actors involved in peace negotiations, is prohibited.

Parties shall refrain from manipulating, corrupting, poisoning, falsifying, deleting, or otherwise compromising the integrity or reliability of Data belonging to civilians, humanitarian actors, public institutions, or other protected persons or entities.

The Parties commit to exercising control over the following Proxy Actors to prevent their commission of Prohibited Digital Operations under the terms of this Agreement: [Proxy Actor 1]; [Proxy Actor 2]; [Proxy Actor 3].

Parties shall bear responsibility for breaches of this Agreement committed by Proxy Actors over which each Party agrees it has control. This responsibility applies regardless of the territory from which the Prohibited Digital Operations are carried out.

The Parties agree not to support, finance, equip, train, or otherwise facilitate Proxy Actors to conduct Prohibited Digital Operations and will take all reasonable and appropriate steps to prevent and disrupt Prohibited Digital Operations by Proxy Actors.
The Parties shall refrain from working with Cyber Mercenaries to engage in Prohibited Digital Operations which violate this Agreement.
The Parties agree to take reasonable steps to prevent Third Party States from undermining this Agreement, to the extent the Parties are able to do so.

Parties agree not to direct, support, or encourage Information and Communications Technology Companies, satellite operators, cloud providers, AI companies, and other Digital Infrastructure providers to engage in Prohibited Digital Operations or to use, or knowingly allow their products or services to be used, for such purposes, which include but are not limited to Internet Shutdowns, Online Incitement to Violence, and purchasing Online Advertisements that undermine peace.

The Parties agree that the purposes underlying Permissible Digital Operations are to mitigate the effects of the {{o-context}} on civilians and affected areas, to mobilize public support for Digital Peace, to encourage Confidence Building Measures by the Parties, and to ensure compliance with the terms of this Agreement.
The Parties agree to the following Permissible Digital Operations:

Ensuring that populations are connected to an open and available internet, able to access life saving information and emergency services online, and that internet users’ rights are respected online and offline.

Publishing online content that supports and enables humanitarian services, access to aid, and the facilitation of life-saving information such as the location of safe zones and humanitarian corridors, including from the United Nations, international humanitarian organizations, and civil society organizations.
Supporting media and social media narratives to endorse an end to violence and the achievement of peaceful solutions, and spread a message of de-escalation and tolerance.
Harmonizing technical standards across borders and between Parties, for example by standardizing spectrum, television signals, and other forms of Digital broadcasting.

Leveraging technologies to: enhance a shared understanding of both the Digital and traditional elements of the {{o-context}}; facilitate communication between the Parties, Proxy Actors, Third Parties, and the public; and provide negotiators with essential Data and information to support the implementation of this Agreement.

Implementing strictly defensive cybersecurity measures to protect systems, networks, and Data from unauthorized access and disruption, and taking action to reverse threats, including removing Malware already implanted in the other Party’s networks.
Responsibly disclosing knowledge about vulnerabilities in the other Party’s hardware or software that were used to gain access to their networks.
Undertaking activities to secure, repair, or restore critical Digital Infrastructure, including networks, Data systems, and essential services.
Securing, backing up, or restoring Data essential to humanitarian efforts and civilian life, including medical, identity, and other civilian records.
Undertaking Digital Confidence Building Measures that enhance transparency, reduce misperception, and enable communication.
Other Permissible Digital Operations may be agreed upon by the Parties.
The Parties agree to a Monitoring Commission with the following composition:
The Parties agree that the following {{o-entity}} shall compose the Monitoring Commission: [entity 1]; [entity 2]; [entity 3].
The Parties agree that {{o-entity}} shall name a Chairperson to oversee the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission shall be responsible for determining what structure and personnel will best enable it to fulfill its roles.

The Parties understand that the Monitoring Commission may recruit representatives from non-profit organizations, academic institutions, and Information and Communication Technology Companies to contribute to fulfilling the Monitoring Commission’s roles.
The Parties agree to appoint their own representatives in the relevant sectors to respond to and collaborate with the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree to a Monitoring Commission with the following role(s):
The Parties are committed to sharing relevant and accurate information with the Monitoring Commission upon its request.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission will serve as an intermediary for information sharing between the Parties of potential and actual breaches to the Agreement.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may create a mechanism to share information regarding alleged or actual breaches of the Agreement with the public.

[State] Parties agree that their national telecommunications regulatory bodies will share with the Monitoring Commission, or provide upon its request, information regarding Internet Interference from their territories and Internet Interference committed by Proxy Actors.

[State] Parties agree that their national intelligence agencies will share with the Monitoring Commission, or provide upon its request, information regarding Information Threats from their territories and Information Threats committed by Proxy Actors.

[State] Parties agree that their Computer Emergency Response Teams (CERTS) and Computer Incident Security Response Teams (CSIRTS) will share with the Commission, or provide upon its request, information regarding potential Cyber Attacks from their territories and Cyber Attacks committed by Proxy Actors.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for monitoring compliance with this Agreement.
The Parties agree that monitoring means observing and recording events or actions related to this Agreement without making formal judgments about the Parties’ compliance with this Agreement.

The Parties understand that the Monitoring Commission is unable to monitor most potential breaches with absolute certainty, and that the confidence with which it monitors breaches will depend on the type of possible breach (Internet Interference, Information Threat, or Cyber Attack), the information available about the possible breach, and the technical capacity of the monitors.

The Parties authorize the Monitoring Commission to establish a mechanism by which Parties and non-parties can report potential breaches of this Agreement. Non-parties may include civil society organizations, international actors, and affected civilians.
The Parties agree that the Commission shall be responsible for establishing a process and timeline to notify the Parties of any Party’s perceived breaches to the Agreement.

The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Commission may request that Information and Communication Technology Companies provide information designed to help monitor breaches. Such requests may include, but are not limited to, information on: Cyber Attacks using a company’s tools or infrastructure; a Party to the Agreement demanding the company enact an Internet Shutdown; a Party’s or Proxy Actor’s use of a social media or communications platform for Online Incitement to Violence.
The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Commission may request cooperation from Third Party States.
The Parties agree to monitor their own compliance with the Agreement and to notify the Monitoring Commission of their own potential breaches to its provisions.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for verifying whether allegations of breaches reported to or observed by the Monitoring Commission are indeed breaches.

The Parties agree that verification means assessing or confirming whether the Parties are complying with this Agreement based on information observed by the Monitoring Commission or provided to the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties understand that to address instances where the Monitoring Commission is unable to verify and attribute potential breaches with absolute certainty, the Monitoring Commission may set percentage confidence thresholds (e.g. 80%) for each potential type of breach (e.g. Online Incitement to Violence) to be attributed to a particular Party. The Parties understand this percentage confidence threshold is likely to vary based on whether the breach concerns Internet Interference, Information Threats, or Cyber Attacks, and based on the incident and information available.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for reporting all {{o-verified}} breaches to the Agreement.

The Parties agree that reporting means sharing information about {{o-verified}} breaches of this Agreement with the public – using a structured, impartial, and evidence-based format that balances transparency, neutrality, and the protection of sensitive information. The Parties understand these reports are essential for documenting compliance, informing the public, and preventing escalation.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission has good offices to help resolve disputes between the Parties to this Agreement.
If the Parties have questions about what constitutes a breach to the provisions of this Agreement, they can reach out to the Monitoring Commission for clarification.
The Parties agree that the announcement of this Agreement shall be disseminated by the Parties through command channels with written orders requiring compliance.

The Parties agree that the announcement of this Agreement will be communicated to the civilian population via print, radio, electronic media, social media and all other possible means of communication. Announcements will be made in the appropriate languages and translated as needed.
The Parties agree to disseminate the announcement of this Agreement to all relevant Third Parties, including Proxy Actors, and other actors who should be aware of the Agreement.

The Parties agree to communicate to their personnel, Proxy Actors, relevant Third Parties, the civilian population, civil society organizations, and the international community that the failure to comply with this Agreement is likely to result in renewed Prohibited Digital Operations and the breakdown of trust between the Parties.
The Parties agree to disseminate the announcement of this Agreement to and engage with Information and Communication Technology Companies to promote compliance with and support for this Agreement.
The Parties shall provide accurate information concerning this Agreement to the media and shall not interfere with the dissemination of information about this Agreement.
The Parties shall give notice of this Agreement to the appropriate international and regional organizations.
The Parties welcome the commitment(s) of [financial supporter 1], [financial supporter 2], [financial supporter 3] to help implement this Agreement and to finance the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties call upon [financial supporter 1], [financial supporter 2], [financial supporter 3] to provide the necessary resources to help implement this Agreement and to finance the Monitoring Commission.

Parties to this Agreement understand that Party representative signatures are required to bring the Agreement into force. Signatories must have the authority to conclude such an Agreement on behalf of the Party.
Third Parties serving as {{o-mediators}} shall include their signatures to ensure compliance with this Agreement.
